question: Photo: Cornea with macrostriae post refractive surgery, how many weeks post op?
explanation: When present, macrostriae almost always become apparent in the early postoperative period. It is important to recognize and address this complication early, as the success of interventions decreases greatly over time, and this problem can cause visually significant irregular astigmatism. The surgeon must examine the surgical eye(s) carefully to check for the presence of gross fullthickness folds (intraoperatively) or flap slippage (postoperatively).- AAO. Note, though no specific time mentioned, will go with A.

review.explanation: Macrostriae are full-thickness folds caused by slippage of the LASIK flap, and they are almost always apparent on the first postoperative day, with virtually all cases presenting inside the first week. Early recognition is essential because lifting, refloating and stretching the flap, sometimes with hypotonic saline or sutures, becomes far less effective once the folds have set, leaving visually significant irregular astigmatism. The later time points do not fit the natural history at all.
review.concern: The option set is expressed in weeks whereas macrostriae are typically a day-one finding, so 1 to 2 weeks is chosen as the only option consistent with the early time course.

question: Large salmon patch of the conjunctiva, no systemic involvement. treatment:
explanation: The mainstay of treatment for localized lymphoma is external beam radiation therapy. Lesion must be biopsied first. - AAO

referenceLinks.title: Conjunctival Lymphoma — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Describes the mobile non-lobulated salmon-pink patch of EMZL and states EBRT is the treatment of choice for indolent EMZL/FL (20-50 Gy over ~15 fractions, ~80% progression-free at 5 years). Text only, no figures

referenceLinks.title: Conjunctival extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of MALT in the fornix — PMC (open access)
referenceLinks.shows: Slit-lamp photographs of forniceal conjunctival lymphoma revealed by strong lid eversion in three cases, plus histopathology/immunohistochemistry; all treated with radiotherapy 30 Gy in 15 fractions with no recurrence

referenceLinks.title: "Salmon Patch": An Indicator of Conjunctival Lymphoma — PMC (open access)
referenceLinks.shows: Clinical photo of a painless salmon-coloured mucosal swelling of the inferior palpebral conjunctiva, with CD20-positive lymphocytic infiltrate on biopsy

figureFinding: Conjunctival lymphoma — a smooth, mobile, salmon-pink patch of bulbar conjunctiva or fornix. Localized disease with no systemic involvement is treated with external beam radiotherapy.

review.explanation: A salmon-pink conjunctival infiltrate is lymphoid tissue, and a large lesion confined to the conjunctiva with no systemic disease is treated with external beam radiotherapy once incisional biopsy has established histology and immunophenotype and systemic staging has been completed. Observation is inappropriate for a confirmed lymphoma, complete excision is unrealistic for a large diffuse lesion and would leave positive margins, and systemic chemotherapy is reserved for systemic disease. Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia is clinically indistinguishable, which is precisely why the biopsy comes first.

question: Most likely pic that needs a scrape:

options.B: pic with very red eye and large central infiltrate

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: A large central infiltrate in a markedly inflamed eye is presumed infectious keratitis threatening the visual axis, and that is the classic indication to scrape for smear and culture before starting fortified therapy. Marginal keratitis is a sterile staphylococcal hypersensitivity infiltrate sitting near the limbus with a clear zone of separation from it, and scraping it yields nothing; a scar is inactive tissue with nothing to grow. The usual thresholds for culturing are a central location, size of about 2 mm or more, deep stromal involvement, an atypical appearance, or failure of empirical treatment.

question: See the image below.
explanation: The exact pathogenesis of OCP remains to be elucidated but the existing evidence supports a Type II hypersensitivity response caused by an autoantibody to a cell surface antigen in the basement membrane of the conjunctival epithelium and other similar squamous epithelia. - Eyewiki

referenceLinks.title: Ocular Cicatricial Pemphigoid — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Photos of the stages of OCP, symblepharon in the inferior fornix, advanced end-stage disease with surface keratinization, and complete ocular surface keratinization; text gives the anti-beta-4 integrin autoantibody / complement-mediated cytotoxic mechanism and Mondino staging

referenceLinks.title: Ocular Cicatricial Pemphigoid: atypical presentation — EyeRounds (University of Iowa)
referenceLinks.shows: External photos of pseudopterygium and limbal stem cell deficiency in an atypical OCP case, plus comparison photos of classic stage 3 symblepharon and stage 4 cicatricial ankyloblepharon with keratinization

figureFinding: Ocular cicatricial pemphigoid (mucous membrane pemphigoid): cicatrizing conjunctivitis with subepithelial fibrosis, fornix foreshortening, symblepharon and ultimately keratinization/ankyloblepharon. Mechanism is a type II hypersensitivity — autoantibody against the beta-4 subunit of alpha-6/beta-4 integrin in the basement membrane, with complement activation.

review.explanation: Ocular cicatricial pemphigoid is an autoantibody-mediated type II hypersensitivity reaction, in which autoantibodies, typically against the beta-4 subunit of integrin in the epithelial basement membrane zone, bind a fixed cell-surface or matrix antigen and trigger complement activation and inflammatory cell recruitment. The result is subepithelial fibrosis with fornix foreshortening, symblepharon, entropion with trichiasis and eventual keratinisation, and the diagnosis is confirmed by conjunctival biopsy with direct immunofluorescence showing linear deposition at the basement membrane zone. Type I is immediate IgE-mediated allergy, type III is immune complex deposition, and type IV is the delayed cell-mediated response of contact dermatitis and phlyctenulosis.
review.concern: The record is corrupted: the stem is missing and the second option is a fragment of the following question rather than a genuine answer choice. The medicine, that ocular cicatricial pemphigoid is a type II hypersensitivity, is solid regardless.

question: Patient with chemical burn 8 months ago, on exam conj scarring/fibrosis, keratinization, and corneal haze. What is the best option for this patient?
explanation: For unilateral, moderate, or severe chemical injuries, a limbal autograft can be obtained from the healthy fellow eye. - AAO

referenceLinks.title: Limbal Stem Cell Deficiency — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Clinical photos of partial and full conjunctivalization courtesy of LV Prasad Eye Institute, an LSCD causes diagram, limbal explant culture and SLET images; chemical/thermal burns listed as acquired causes with scarring, keratinization and calcification

referenceLinks.title: Simple Limbal Epithelial Transplantation (SLET) — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Photo of unilateral LSCD after an alkali (oven cleaner) burn, palisades of Vogt diagram, step-by-step surgical technique photos, and serial pre-op through 6-month post-op photos of an eye treated after an acid injury

figureFinding: Total limbal stem cell deficiency after a chemical burn: conjunctivalization and superficial vascularization of the cornea, late conjunctival scarring/fibrosis with keratinization, and corneal haze — treated with limbal epithelial (stem cell) transplantation.

review.explanation: Conjunctival scarring with keratinisation and corneal haze eight months after a chemical burn is limbal stem cell deficiency, in which conjunctival epithelium with its vessels and goblet cells replaces the corneal epithelium. The surface must be rehabilitated with limbal stem cell transplantation, a limbal autograft from the healthy fellow eye in unilateral injury or cultivated limbal epithelial transplantation, before any keratoplasty is contemplated. Penetrating or lamellar keratoplasty performed on a stem-cell-deficient surface will not epithelialise and will fail. A keratoprosthesis is reserved for end-stage bilateral disease in which stem cell grafting has failed or is not feasible.

question: Corneal ulcer post-trauma with negative scrape, next step?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: When scrapings are negative and a post-traumatic ulcer is not resolving, the organisms being missed are typically deep or sequestered, fungi and Acanthamoeba in particular, and the next step is to obtain deeper tissue by corneal biopsy for histology and culture on appropriate media. Confocal microscopy, where available, is a sensible non-invasive adjunct beforehand. A trial of topical or systemic corticosteroid in an undiagnosed infectious keratitis risks fulminant progression and perforation, and viral culture is a narrow test for an organism that a history of trauma with an ulcer does not particularly suggest.

question: Mature cataract with cells, no KPs, AC Grade 3, pic showing corneal haze, what type of glaucoma
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: A mature or hypermature cataract with a heavy anterior chamber reaction, raised pressure and an intact capsule is phacolytic glaucoma, in which high-molecular-weight lens proteins leak through a microscopically intact capsule and are engulfed by macrophages that then obstruct the trabecular meshwork. The absence of keratic precipitates is the deliberate clue separating it from phacoantigenic uveitis, which follows capsular rupture and is granulomatous with keratic precipitates. Phacomorphic glaucoma is an angle closure from an intumescent lens and would show a shallow chamber, and lens particle glaucoma requires free cortical material in the anterior chamber after capsular disruption from surgery or trauma. Definitive treatment is cataract extraction once pressure and inflammation are controlled.

question: Patient post cataract surgery came for a follow up. You noticed a white sheet representing epithelial ingrowth. How will you confirm?
explanation: If the diagnosis is in question, a spot of argon laser photocoagulation is applied to the area overlying the iris. - Eyewiki

review.explanation: Epithelial downgrowth appears as a translucent membrane with a scalloped advancing edge across the endothelium, angle and iris, and the classic confirmatory test is to apply low-energy argon laser burns to the part of the sheet lying on the iris surface, where the epithelium blanches white while normal iris does not. This both confirms the diagnosis and maps the extent before any surgical intervention. A dye test at the wound, that is a Seidel test, detects the fistula or wound leak that often accompanies downgrowth but does not identify the membrane itself; anterior segment OCT and specular or confocal microscopy are useful adjuncts.

question: During cataract surgery: tense eye, absent red reflex, lens rising, next step:
explanation: OphthoQ:

referenceLinks.title: Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Lists the intraoperative signs (anterior chamber shallowing, loss of red reflex, raised IOP with firming of the globe, spontaneous nuclear expression, iris and vitreous prolapse) and states immediate tamponade by closure of all incisions. Text only, no figures

referenceLinks.title: Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage as a Complication of Routine Cataract Surgery — Moran CORE (University of Utah)
referenceLinks.shows: Six surgical videos: posterior capsule folds during epinuclear removal, positive pressure on viscoelastic injection, wound hydration to pressurize the eye, plus example clips of an SCH with loss of red reflex during phaco and an expulsive haemorrhage during keratoplasty

figureFinding: Intraoperative (expulsive) suprachoroidal haemorrhage during cataract surgery: rock-hard eye, shallowing anterior chamber, posterior capsule bulging forward, loss of the red reflex and the lens/iris/vitreous prolapsing out of the wound. Immediate management is to close all wounds and pressurize the eye.

review.explanation: A suddenly firm eye with loss of the red reflex, a shallowing chamber and forward displacement of the lens and iris during surgery is an expulsive suprachoroidal haemorrhage, and the immediate action is to close the incision and restore a closed, pressurised globe so that the rising intraocular pressure tamponades the bleeding, using digital pressure and rapid sutures. Continuing to remove the lens or injecting fluid risks extrusion of intraocular contents. Posterior sclerotomy was historically advocated but is no longer the first move and can worsen the bleed; drainage, if ever needed, is done later, usually at 7 to 14 days once the clot has liquefied.

question: What do you do after placing an anterior segment IOL after PC Rupture and anterior vitrectomy:
explanation: Usually, the IOL haptics are at 3 and 9 o'clock and the PI is at 12 o'clock. Done intraop to prevent iris bombe. Picture of unilateral Arcus, what to do?

review.explanation: An anterior chamber intraocular lens sits with its haptics at roughly 3 and 9 o'clock and impedes aqueous flow enough that a peripheral iridectomy is required to prevent pupillary block and iris bombe, and it is made at the time of surgery rather than deferred, because the pressure can spike on the first postoperative day. A superior position at 12 o'clock keeps it clear of the haptics and, being covered by the upper lid, avoids the glare and dysphotopsia that an inferior iridectomy produces. Relying on a postoperative laser iridotomy leaves the patient unprotected in the interim and may be difficult through a hazy, inflamed eye.

question: Hyphema which of the following is uncommon:

options.A: Mostly treated with bed rest and head elevation
options.D: Rebleeding commonly occurs after the third week

explanation: From the following choices, D is uncommon, as rebleeding most commonly occurs within the first 5 to 10 days. Reference: The Wills Eye Manual (Page 69)

referenceLinks.title: Hyphema — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Seven clinical figures: 1 mm hyphema with corneal edema and Descemet folds after airbag trauma, slit-beam views of layered blood, hyphema from iris neovascularization, grade 3 hyphema after a firecracker blast, total hyphema, and a rebleed with fresh red blood over a dark clot. Text gives blunt trauma as the commonest cause, the 0-IV grading, IOP risk by grade (13.5% grade I-II vs 52% grade IV), head elevation at least 45 degrees, and rebleeding usually within the first 5 days

figureFinding: Traumatic hyphema — layered blood in the anterior chamber after blunt trauma, and a rebleed (fresh bright red blood over an older dark clot). The exam point is that rebleeding happens in the first 3-5 days, NOT after the third week.

review.explanation: Rebleeding after traumatic hyphema characteristically occurs in the first few days, most often between days 2 and 5 and almost always within the first week, as the clot retracts and lyses, and it is the single event that most worsens prognosis. A rebleed in the third week would be distinctly uncommon, making that the false statement the question is asking you to identify. The other three are true: most hyphemas follow blunt trauma, most are managed conservatively with rest, head elevation, a shield, cycloplegia and topical steroid, and larger hyphemas raise the pressure and can cause glaucoma. Watch particularly for corneal blood staining and screen for sickle cell haemoglobinopathy, in which even moderate pressure elevation is dangerous.

referenceLinks.title: Diabetic Macular Edema — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Thirteen figures including microaneurysms with corresponding OCT, circinate exudates, center- versus non-center-involved DME, focal and diffuse DME on fluorescein angiography, and focal and grid laser treatment planning/parameters; also shows pseudophakic (Irvine-Gass) CME for contrast

referenceLinks.title: Cataract — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Three slit-lamp images of posterior subcapsular cataract, including retroillumination of a small central PSC and PSC in a 16-year-old with insulin-dependent diabetes; text on glare and near-vision symptoms

figureFinding: Diabetic macular oedema (leaking microaneurysms, circinate exudates, cystoid thickening on OCT) coexisting with a posterior subcapsular cataract — DME is treated first, then phaco once the oedema has resolved.

review.explanation: Cataract surgery in a diabetic eye with active macular oedema reliably worsens the oedema, so the macula is treated first and the lens is removed once the oedema has settled, with roughly three months allowed to judge the response and confirm stability. One month is generally too short to establish resolution, and operating first with macular treatment a week later exposes an oedematous macula to the surgical inflammatory insult. The exception that reverses the priority is a cataract so dense that the macula cannot be assessed or treated, in which case surgery goes first, often with anti-VEGF given at the time of operation.
review.concern: Focal laser has largely been replaced by anti-VEGF for centre-involving diabetic macular oedema; the sequencing principle is what is being tested.

question: IOL of 0 power in myopic patient, what is the benefit of impacting it?
explanation: It is preferable that the patient receive an IOL when possible; the lens implant serves as a barrier to movement of the vitreous base and associated traction on the retina. - AAO

review.explanation: Even when no refractive power is required, implanting the lens is worthwhile because the implant and an intact capsule act as a barrier to forward vitreous movement and to the traction on the vitreous base that produces retinal breaks, and aphakia carries a higher detachment risk than pseudophakia. That matters most in exactly this patient, a high myope whose baseline detachment risk is already elevated. Cystoid macular oedema is driven by inflammation and vitreous incarceration rather than by the presence of an implant, and corneal decompensation relates to endothelial trauma and to anterior chamber lenses, not to a plano posterior chamber implant.

question: Unilateral RB with normal parents, chance of next sibling having RB?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

referenceLinks.title: Retinoblastoma — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Clinical photo captioned 'Leukocoria in a retinoblastoma patient'; RB1 genetics, autosomal dominant with ~90% penetrance, and sibling/offspring screening guidance

referenceLinks.title: Category:Retinoblastoma — Wikimedia Commons
referenceLinks.shows: Openly licensed leukocoria photo, a 'Fundus of retinoblastoma' subcategory, ultrasound, MRI, and gross/histopathology of RB

figureFinding: Retinoblastoma — leukocoria / white fundus tumour. Same genetic counselling point as promotion-2021#15: sporadic unilateral RB with unaffected parents gives siblings roughly 1-2% risk.

review.explanation: Unilateral retinoblastoma with unaffected parents and no family history is sporadic and somatic in roughly 85 percent of cases, so the risk to a sibling is small, on the order of 1 to 2 percent. The residual risk reflects the minority of unilateral cases that do carry a germline mutation and the rare unaffected parent with a low-penetrance or mosaic allele. Risks near 50 percent apply to the offspring of a patient with heritable disease, which is typically bilateral or multifocal, and germline testing of the proband converts these population figures into a precise risk for the family.

question: 3yr old boy Patient referred from peadiatric after he was diagnosed with Usher syndrome based on hearing loss and vestibular finding. On examination you found XT 35 PD. what is the most appropriate next diagnostics step?
explanation: Genetic Testing: Definitive diagnosis of Usher Syndrome type 1 involves identifying a homozygous proband mutation in the setting of positive symptoms and family history. The first gene to identify using single-gene sequencing is MYO7A. - Eyewiki

review.explanation: Usher syndrome is retinitis pigmentosa with congenital sensorineural hearing loss, and type 1, the form with profound deafness plus vestibular areflexia as described here, is confirmed by identifying biallelic mutations, MYO7A being the first gene to sequence. At three years the fundus may still look near normal, so molecular confirmation is the decisive diagnostic step and it also guides prognosis and family counselling. Double Maddox rod measures cyclotorsion and is irrelevant, and CT of the brain does not address an inherited retinal and cochlear disorder; the exotropia is sensory, secondary to poor vision.
review.concern: A full-field ERG remains the traditional confirmatory test in a young child, being extinguished long before fundus changes appear, and would arguably be the better next step, but it is not among the options.

question: HQC toxicity, how to investigate:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Current screening for hydroxychloroquine retinopathy rests on two primary tests, automated visual fields and spectral domain OCT, using the 10-2 pattern for most patients with the 24-2 or 30-2 added for patients of Asian descent, in whom the damage is often extramacular. Of the options offered, OCT is the primary objective structural test, showing parafoveal outer retinal and ellipsoid zone loss, the flying saucer appearance, before the patient is symptomatic. Full-field ERG only becomes abnormal in advanced widespread disease, and fluorescein angiography has no screening role at all.
review.concern: Multifocal ERG is a legitimate and sensitive objective adjunct, endorsed for corroborating equivocal fields, so a reasonable case can be made for it; SD-OCT remains the primary structural screening test and the intended answer.

question: Baseline evaluation for patients beginning treatment with a chloroquine derivative should include a complete ophthalmic examination. For follow-up comparison, the ophthalmologist should employ SD- OCT as well as automated threshold field testing with a white pattern (Humphrey white 10-2 protocol) - AAO OphthaQ:

options.B: RD + with high IOP (not responding to antiglaucoma):

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Schwartz-Matsuo syndrome is a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, usually with a peripheral break or dialysis and often post-traumatic, in which photoreceptor outer segments migrate through the break into the anterior chamber and obstruct the trabecular meshwork, raising the pressure. The cells seen in the anterior chamber are mistaken for uveitis, and neither corticosteroids nor pressure-lowering drops resolve the problem; the pressure normalises once the detachment is repaired. Think of it whenever raised pressure and anterior chamber cells accompany a detachment, because the treatment is retinal surgery rather than glaucoma surgery.
review.concern: The record is corrupted, with the stem missing and the second option carrying a fragment of the actual question. Answered on the reading that the question asked for the diagnosis in a retinal detachment with raised pressure unresponsive to antiglaucoma therapy.

question: Patient was referred to r/o RD OD. O/E ERD. FFA showed leopard spot pattern without leakage, hx of lung cancer in the family. What is the association:
explanation: AAO:

review.explanation: An exudative detachment with a leopard-spot pattern on fluorescein angiography and no frank leakage points to chronic disturbance at the level of the choroid and retinal pigment epithelium, and uveal effusion syndrome is the classic entity, with serous choroidal and retinal detachment, shifting subretinal fluid, and the mottled hyper- and hypofluorescence of long-standing RPE change; it is associated with nanophthalmos, hyperopia and abnormally thickened sclera. Cancer-associated retinopathy is a paraneoplastic photoreceptor degeneration that presents with photopsias, nyctalopia, ring scotomas and an extinguished ERG, not with an exudative detachment, so the cancer history is the distractor here.
review.concern: Worth flagging that bilateral diffuse uveal melanocytic proliferation, a paraneoplastic syndrome of systemic carcinoma including lung cancer, also produces exudative detachment with a leopard-spot or giraffe pattern. It would become the answer if the malignancy were the patient's own rather than a family member's, and if the third option is a garbled rendering of a diffuse uveal melanocytic process rather than simple choroidal pigmentation.

question: elderly htn and dm with unilateral low va and pain 2 days has dilated retinal veins and hemorrhages, rubeosis, corneal edema, other eye only mild microaneurysms.
explanation: In OIS the retinal veins are dilated and irregular in caliber. The retinal arterioles are narrowed. Associated findings include midperipheral retinal hemorrhages (80%), iris neovascularization (66%), and posterior segment neovascularization (37%). Child trauma with metal hanger, picture of optic nerve avulsion (dark ON with surrounding hemorrhage) dx?

referenceLinks.title: Ocular Ischemic Syndrome — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Fifteen figures including fundus photo and fluorescein angiogram of OIS microaneurysms, a gonioscopic view of rubeosis iridis, FA showing prolonged retinal and choroidal filling, ICG, carotid duplex/MRA/arteriography of ICA occlusion; Table 2 compares OIS versus CRVO versus diabetic retinopathy point by point

referenceLinks.title: Ocular Ischemic Syndrome — StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)
referenceLinks.shows: Frequencies of the classic signs (dilated non-tortuous veins 90%, retinal haemorrhages 80%, rubeosis iridis 67%) and the explicit CRVO discriminator — in CRVO veins are dilated AND tortuous, and delayed choroidal filling on FA favours OIS

figureFinding: Ocular ischemic syndrome: unilateral vision loss with dull ocular/orbital ache ('ocular angina'), narrowed arterioles with dilated but NON-tortuous retinal veins, round deep mid-peripheral dot-blot haemorrhages, microaneurysms, rubeosis iridis with corneal oedema — with the fellow eye showing only mild background diabetic change.

review.explanation: Ocular ischemic syndrome is the unifying diagnosis: pain, dilated but non-tortuous veins, mid-peripheral hemorrhages, corneal edema and rubeosis in one eye of an elderly vasculopath, while the fellow eye shows only mild background diabetic change. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is a bilateral, roughly symmetric disease, so a fellow eye with only scattered microaneurysms argues strongly against it. Branch retinal vein occlusion produces a sectoral, wedge-shaped hemorrhage pattern respecting the horizontal raphe and is rarely painful or associated with rubeosis of this degree. The combination of ocular pain (from ischemia and raised pressure) with marked interocular asymmetry is the classic examination-room signature of carotid occlusive disease.

question: CMV retinitis monitoring:

options.A: AF of the edge of active retinitis

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: CMV retinitis is monitored by serially documenting the leading border of the necrotic lesion, because progression is defined as advancement of that edge; imaging the edge of active retinitis is therefore the correct monitoring strategy. Serial photographs of vitritis are useless because immunosuppressed patients with low CD4 counts mount little vitreous inflammation, and the vitreous haze does not track disease activity. Fluorescein angiography adds nothing beyond what is visible clinically and exposes the patient to unnecessary dye. The nuance worth teaching is that the historical gold standard is serial wide-field colour fundus photography of the lesion border; autofluorescence of the border is a modern adjunct that highlights the transition from active necrosis to atrophic scar.

question: Patient with uveitis and +3 AC cells on PF Q4hr and 33 mmHg IOP comes for a follow up with +4 AC cells and 28 mmHg IOP, next step:

options.A: Decrease PF to once daily and give latanoprost QHS
options.B: Decrease PF to once daily and give timolol BID
options.C: Increase PF to Q2hr and give latanoprost QHS
options.D: Increase PF to Q2hr and give timolol BID

explanation: C C D B c C OphthaQ: herpetic uveitis is generally associated with more inflammation and discomfort. Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is more insidious without episodic attacks of elevated IOP. The rest are not typically associated with high IOP onset in which the vitreous is the primary site of inflammatio. Management : Systemic steroids. This modality is preferred over regional steroid by some practitioners if symptomatic inflammation is bilateral. The figure depicts cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis in an HIV-positive patient. CMV retinitis is the most common ocular opportunistic infection in patients with AIDS (and is an AIDS-defining illness). CMV retinitis usually occurs when CD4 + count drops below 50 cells/μL. Patients present with blurry vision and/or floaters. Clinically, the retina appears white and may have intraretinal hemorrhage, exudate, necrosis, periphlebitis, or "frosted-branch" angiitis. Options for systemic coverage include high-dose induction with either intravenous ganciclovir (5 mg/kg twice daily) or foscarnet (90 mg/kg twice daily) for 2 weeks, followed by low-dose daily maintenance therapy or oral valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily) for 3 weeks, followed by maintenance therapy (900 mg/day). Source : self assessment Explenation : Several studies have invesFgated what is the opFmal IOL for paFents with uveiFs. In adults, it has been shown that various materials such as acrylic and hydrogel are relaFvely safe with a favorable outcome however, seen with with acrylic IOLs Category : Uveitis Reference: kanski , ophthoquestion Category : Uveitis

review.explanation: The inflammation has worsened from 3+ to 4+ cells despite prednisolone every four hours, so the steroid must be intensified rather than tapered; under-treated uveitis is itself a cause of trabeculitis and secondary pressure elevation. The pressure remains above target at 28 mmHg, so an aqueous suppressant is added, and timolol is the appropriate choice. Prostaglandin analogues such as latanoprost are relatively contraindicated in active uveitis because they can aggravate intraocular inflammation and promote cystoid macular oedema. Both options that reduce prednisolone to once daily would allow the uveitis to escalate further, which is exactly the wrong direction given a rising cell count.

question: After trauma patient had 25% hyphema that resolved within one week, for several months he had IOP of 5 might, then all of a sudden he had high IOP of 57mmgh, what could be the cause:
explanation: More than half of eyes (12/18 and 13/17 in two case series) experience a period of significant, often painful IOP elevation following successful closure of a cyclodialysis cleft.[19] [20] This is typically self-limited and can be managed with topical IOP-lowering drops with or without oral CAIs, systemic osmotics, and oral analgesics. - Eyewiki

referenceLinks.title: Cyclodialysis Clefts — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Gonioscopic photos of cyclodialysis clefts after paintball injuries in two eyes, plus a UBM demonstrating the cleft; text states more than half of eyes (12/18 and 13/17 in two series) get a significant, often painful IOP elevation after successful cleft closure, and that hypotony (IOP 5 mmHg or less) after blunt trauma with hyphema should raise suspicion

figureFinding: Cyclodialysis cleft after blunt trauma: ciliary body detached from the scleral spur, seen on gonioscopy as a deep angle recess opening into the suprachoroidal space (confirmed on UBM). It causes chronic hypotony, and when the cleft spontaneously closes the IOP spikes sharply.

review.explanation: The narrative is diagnostic: blunt trauma, then months of pressure around 5 mmHg, which points to a cyclodialysis cleft allowing direct suprachoroidal outflow and suppressed aqueous production. When such a cleft closes, either spontaneously or after treatment, the eye abruptly regains its aqueous load against an outflow system that has been dormant, producing a dramatic and often painful pressure spike into the fifties. Ghost cell glaucoma follows a vitreous haemorrhage by weeks, presents with khaki-coloured cells in the anterior chamber, and would not be preceded by months of hypotony. Angle recession glaucoma develops insidiously over years with a gradually rising pressure and never explains the preceding prolonged hypotony.

question: Patient with ocular melanoma post radiation treatment. VA 20/100, had high IOP despite being on full antiglaucoma medication. What to do?
explanation: Surgical intervention should only be considered if the patient failed more conservative treatment options. Transscleral cyclophotocoagulation or cryotherapy to the ciliary body offer less invasive ways to control IOP.[1][42][43] Incisional glaucoma surgery, including filtration procedures and aqueous tube shunts, are generally contraindicated, except in cases of metastases, due to the potential risk of facilitating tumor spread outside of the globe. - Eyewiki

review.explanation: In an eye harbouring a uveal melanoma, filtering procedures and tube shunts create a direct transscleral conduit and are avoided because of the theoretical risk of seeding tumour cells into the subconjunctival space and orbit. Transscleral cyclophotocoagulation lowers pressure without creating such a fistula, which makes it the preferred surgical option once maximal medical therapy has failed. Simply observing on full medical therapy is not acceptable when the pressure remains uncontrolled, since the eye still has useful vision at 20/100 and the nerve is at risk. The usual sequence in practice is to treat any underlying radiation-induced neovascular component with anti-VEGF and panretinal photocoagulation first, then proceed to cyclodestruction if the pressure remains high.

question: 50y/o patient with high Iop in the right eye and stellate kp and corneal edema on gonio there is also kp's he admits to having a previous similar episode months ago. What is the most important initial treatment that can be instituted in the ER?
explanation: Glaucomatocyclitic Crisis: Initial treatment is directed towards controlling intraocular pressure and decreasing inflammation. Typical first-line therapeutics include topical beta- blockers such as timolol, alpha-agonists such as brimonidine, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as dorzolamide. -Eyewiki

referenceLinks.title: Glaucomatocyclitic Crisis (Posner-Schlossman Syndrome) — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Figure of small, white, discrete keratic precipitates; iris angiogram showing focal iris ischaemia during an attack; trabecular meshwork electron microscopy; serial visual fields

referenceLinks.title: Posner-Schlossman Syndrome — StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)
referenceLinks.shows: IOP elevated to 40 mmHg or above with fine non-granulomatous KPs; first-line IOP reduction in an acute attack is topical beta-blockers, alpha agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, with topical steroids for the (usually mild) inflammation

figureFinding: Posner-Schlossman syndrome (glaucomatocyclitic crisis): recurrent unilateral episodes of markedly high IOP with corneal oedema, few fine non-pigmented KPs on the endothelium, and an open angle with KPs on gonioscopy.

review.explanation: Recurrent unilateral episodes of markedly raised pressure with stellate keratic precipitates, corneal oedema and minimal cell describe glaucomatocyclitic crisis, and the immediate threat to the eye in the emergency room is the pressure itself. Aqueous suppressants, with a topical beta blocker as the standard first agent, act fastest to protect the optic nerve and clear the epithelial oedema. Topical steroid is certainly part of definitive management and is usually started at the same visit, but it does not lower pressure acutely and its benefit accrues over days. Prostaglandins and miotics are avoided in this inflammatory setting, and the question is asking specifically what is most important to institute first.

question: Patient with angle closure glaucoma, you did PI, still high IOP, patient has mild cataract, what is the next step?

options.A: Do phaco because it is phacomorphic
options.B: make sure of the patency of the PI and augment if needed

referenceLinks.title: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Slit-lamp photos of a superior iridotomy at 10 o'clock, a nasal iridotomy seen on transillumination, and an inferior iridotomy in a vitrectomised eye; text warns that transillumination is NOT a reliable indicator of patency and that uncertain patency should be checked with gonioscopy, UBM or AS-OCT while reconsidering the mechanism

referenceLinks.title: Plateau Iris — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Slit-lamp image of a patient with plateau iris syndrome after a patent peripheral iridotomy, gonioscopic view showing anterior bowing of the peripheral iris, and paired UBM images of normal versus plateau anterior chamber anatomy

figureFinding: Angle closure with persistently high IOP despite a laser peripheral iridotomy: the image should show the iridotomy itself (to judge whether it is patent and full thickness) and gonioscopy/UBM of a still-appositionally-closed angle, i.e. plateau iris or another non-pupillary-block mechanism.

review.explanation: When pressure stays high after a peripheral iridotomy the first obligation is to prove the iridotomy is actually patent and of adequate size, best confirmed by transillumination and by seeing the anterior capsule through it; a pigment-plugged or incomplete iridotomy is the commonest reason for apparent failure. Only once patency is confirmed should you go on to consider non-pupillary-block mechanisms such as plateau iris configuration, residual peripheral anterior synechiae, or a lens-related component. A mild cataract by definition is not phacomorphic, so lens extraction on that indication is not justified at this point. Reaching for phacoemulsification before verifying the simplest and most reversible cause is poor surgical judgement.

question: CRVO, HM vision, high IOP, corneal edema, 360 NVI and dense cataract. What to do?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

referenceLinks.title: Neovascular Glaucoma — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Photos of advanced NVG with florid rubeosis iridis, ectropion uveae with hyphema, and gonioscopic neovascularization of the angle; text states cyclophotocoagulation is reserved for eyes with poor visual prognosis (20/400 or worse) and that CRVO plus diabetic retinopathy underlie nearly two-thirds of NVG

figureFinding: Neovascular glaucoma after CRVO: 360 degrees of rubeosis iridis with neovascularization of the angle, corneal oedema, hand-motion vision and a dense cataract. With no view for PRP and no visual potential, transscleral cyclophotocoagulation is the treatment.

review.explanation: This is neovascular glaucoma after central retinal vein occlusion in an eye whose visual potential is hand motions and whose dense cataract and corneal oedema make retinal laser physically impossible. Cyclophotocoagulation lowers pressure and relieves pain without requiring a clear view, and is the standard choice for an uncontrolled neovascular eye with poor visual prognosis. Panretinal photocoagulation is the correct treatment in principle but cannot be delivered through this media, and topical medication alone will not control pressure once the angle is closed by a fibrovascular membrane. Retrobulbar alcohol is reserved for a blind, painful eye as a purely palliative measure, not for an eye still perceiving hand motions. In current practice intravitreal anti-VEGF is given alongside to regress the neovascularisation while the cyclodestruction controls pressure.

question: High IOP 8 weeks post-glaucoma device implant. What is the most common explanation?
explanation: Hypertensive phase

referenceLinks.title: Glaucoma Drainage Devices — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Device/plate anatomy plus a dedicated discussion of the hypertensive phase and capsule encapsulation around the endplate as the cause of IOP rise weeks after implantation

referenceLinks.title: Encapsulated Bleb — Columbia Digital Reference of Ophthalmology
referenceLinks.shows: Clinical photograph captioned 'Encapsulated filtering bleb (Tenon's cyst)' with the associated elevated IOP

figureFinding: Encapsulated bleb (Tenon cyst) over the extraocular plate of a glaucoma drainage device — the tense, dome-shaped, vascularized capsule seen at 4-8 weeks that causes the 'hypertensive phase' of raised IOP

review.explanation: Pressure elevation appearing roughly four to twelve weeks after a glaucoma drainage device is the classic hypertensive phase, caused by a fibrous capsule maturing around the extraocular plate and increasing resistance to aqueous absorption. It is most often seen with valved implants once the plate has been exposed to aqueous for several weeks. Steroid response would typically appear earlier and is diagnosed by the temporal relationship to intensive topical steroid, and persistent inflammation would be accompanied by visible cell and flare. Progressive glaucoma describes worsening optic neuropathy over years and does not explain an abrupt pressure rise at eight weeks in an eye with a functioning drain.

question: Post Phaco + ECP with high IOP and shallow AC (Scenario of Aqueous misdirection) what's of the following is improbable:
explanation: Herpetic uveitis most specific sign

review.explanation: In a shallow-chamber, high-pressure eye after phacoemulsification with endocyclophotocoagulation the differential is pupillary block, suprachoroidal haemorrhage or effusion, and aqueous misdirection. B-scan is genuinely useful here because it excludes a suprachoroidal haemorrhage or effusion, and ultrasound biomicroscopy is the test that demonstrates anteriorly rotated ciliary processes with the lens-iris diaphragm pushed forward. Confirming iridotomy patency is likewise essential, since aqueous misdirection can only be diagnosed once pupillary block has been excluded. Iris bombe is the item that does not fit, because misdirection shallows the chamber uniformly, centrally as well as peripherally, whereas bombe leaves the central chamber relatively deep and is excluded outright by a patent iridotomy.
review.concern: Flagged for reconciliation rather than as a strong override, because the recall is degraded. Two points: the sourceExplanation attached to this item reads Herpetic uveitis most specific sign, which belongs to a different question, so the answer key in this stretch of the document appears misaligned. Second, the same source keys the near-identical 2023 item (promotion-2023#30) as A, contradicting the B given here. On the merits, ordering a B-scan in a shallow-chamber high-pressure post-operative eye is standard care, so B is hard to defend as the improbable option.

question: Patient is Ortho at distant and exophoria at near, +0.25 refraction, what not to give?

options.D: give plus lens more than his refraction

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Orthophoria at distance with exophoria at near and an essentially plano refraction is convergence insufficiency, and the entire treatment strategy is to build fusional convergence. Pencil push-ups, stereograms and base-out prism exercises all load the convergence system and are legitimate orthoptic treatments. Adding plus power beyond the manifest refraction relaxes accommodation, which through the accommodative convergence relationship reduces convergence tone and makes the near exodeviation worse. Plus lenses at near are the correct tool for the opposite problem, a high accommodative convergence to accommodation ratio with esotropia at near.

question: This would increase exophoria.
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Taking the option set at face value, abusive head trauma is the answer to the question these choices belong to, which is the classic infant presentation of multilayered retinal haemorrhages extending to the periphery, often with retinoschisis and perimacular folds. Valsalva retinopathy produces a single sub-internal-limiting-membrane or subhyaloid dome of blood at the macula, typically in an adult after straining. Purtscher retinopathy shows cotton-wool patches and polygonal retinal whitening around the disc after chest compression or long-bone fracture, with relatively few haemorrhages. The pattern and distribution of the haemorrhages, rather than their mere presence, is what distinguishes non-accidental injury.

question: Eye discharge 5 days after birth:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Neonatal conjunctivitis presenting on day five is acquired as the infant passes through an infected birth canal, whether the organism is Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which usually declares itself at two to five days, or Chlamydia trachomatis, which typically appears from day five to fourteen. The mechanism being tested is intrapartum inoculation of the ocular surface, not transplacental spread. Vertical transmission in the sense intended by the distractor means haematogenous transplacental passage, which is how congenital syphilis, rubella and toxoplasmosis reach the fetus and which produces systemic congenital disease rather than an isolated purulent discharge. Onset within the first twenty-four hours would instead suggest chemical conjunctivitis from prophylactic drops.

question: Photo: Post excision of malignant LL mass, how to repair (less than 1/3):
explanation: Small lid defect (less than 25-33%) - direct closure +/- cantholysis Moderate lid defect (33-50%) - Tenzel semicircular rotation flap Large defects (>50%) - Cutler Beard (UL), Hughes (LL)

review.explanation: Eyelid reconstruction is governed by the proportion of the lid margin lost. A defect under about one third can be closed directly, pentagon fashion, in layers, with lateral canthotomy and cantholysis added if the closure is under tension. A Tenzel semicircular rotation flap is brought in for defects of roughly one third to one half. Sharing tissue from the opposing lid, by a Hughes tarsoconjunctival flap for the lower lid or a Cutler-Beard for the upper, is reserved for defects exceeding half the lid, and it has the significant cost of occluding the eye until division, which is unjustifiable for a small defect.

question: Orbital cellulitis with black eschar on nose, What is the organism:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: A black eschar on the nose or palate with orbital involvement is angioinvasive mucormycosis until proven otherwise; the fungus invades vessel walls, produces thrombosis and the resulting infarcted tissue turns necrotic and black. This is a surgical emergency requiring urgent biopsy, systemic amphotericin B, extensive debridement and correction of the underlying ketoacidosis or immunosuppression. Staphylococcus aureus causes a purulent orbital cellulitis with abscess formation but does not produce ischaemic eschar, because it is not angioinvasive in this way. Any diabetic or immunocompromised patient with orbital cellulitis and necrotic tissue must be assumed to have mucormycosis while cultures are pending.

question: Orbital vs preseptal what's the difference:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

referenceLinks.title: Orbital Cellulitis — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Clinical presentation with proptosis, ophthalmoplegia and motility restriction, explicitly contrasted against preseptal disease

referenceLinks.title: Preseptal Cellulitis — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: The contrasting picture — lid oedema and erythema with normal motility and no proptosis

referenceLinks.title: Orbital Cellulitis — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
referenceLinks.shows: States directly that the most important distinguishing feature is ophthalmoplegia, pain with eye movement and/or proptosis

figureFinding: Orbital cellulitis distinguished from preseptal cellulitis: restricted/painful extraocular movements (ophthalmoplegia) and proptosis, with lid swelling common to both

review.explanation: The septum is the anatomical boundary, and what defines postseptal disease is involvement of the orbital contents: restricted or painful eye movement, proptosis, reduced vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, or raised orbital pressure. Limitation of ductions is therefore the discriminating sign among these options. Fever and leucocytosis are systemic inflammatory markers that occur with preseptal cellulitis as well and cannot localise the infection. Two millimetres of proptosis falls within the range of normal interocular asymmetry on exophthalmometry and is too small a difference to be relied upon, whereas any restriction of movement with pain immediately raises the diagnosis to orbital cellulitis and mandates imaging and intravenous antibiotics.

question: Mechanism of TAO:
explanation: Although the underlying mechanisms of action of these processes are not completely understood, the presumed mechanism is activation of orbital fibroblasts by Graves' disease- related autoantibodies. - Eyewiki

review.explanation: Thyroid eye disease is driven by autoantibodies directed at antigens expressed on the orbital fibroblast, principally the thyrotropin receptor with signalling cross-talk through the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor. Activation of that fibroblast leads to hyaluronan secretion, glycosaminoglycan accumulation with osmotic swelling of the extraocular muscles, and adipogenesis in the orbital fat. This shared autoantigen between thyroid and orbit is what explains why the orbit is targeted in Graves disease, and it is the rationale for receptor-directed therapy. There is undeniably a cell-mediated component, with T lymphocyte and macrophage infiltration of the orbit, so option A is not wholly false, but the autoantigen on the fibroblast is the mechanism the question is asking for.

options.B: Poor healing after bleph pic, what could've been done to improve result:

explanation: Factors affecting wound healing

review.explanation: Reading option B as the real stem, the question is what could have been done preoperatively to improve wound healing after blepharoplasty, and tighter glycaemic control is the answer. Hyperglycaemia impairs healing at several points: neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis are blunted, fibroblast proliferation and collagen cross-linking are reduced, and microvascular disease limits tissue oxygenation. The other modifiable factors a surgeon should address before elective lid surgery are smoking, systemic steroid use, malnutrition with low protein and vitamin C, and anticoagulation. Optimising these before the operation is far more effective than trying to rescue a dehisced or poorly healing wound afterwards.

question: VF picture left homonymous hemianpia sparing macula, where is the lesion:
explanation: Left Homonymous Hemianopia with Macular Sparing: Lesions of the occipital lobe will often result in this visual defect. - Eyewiki

review.explanation: A congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing localises to the occipital cortex, because the macular representation at the occipital pole has dual blood supply from the posterior and middle cerebral arteries and is often preserved when the posterior cerebral artery territory infarcts. Lesions of the optic radiations are typically incongruous, and temporal radiation lesions produce the classic pie in the sky superior quadrantanopia without macular sparing. Lateral geniculate lesions give incongruous and characteristically sectoral defects reflecting its dual blood supply. An optic nerve lesion produces a monocular defect with a relative afferent pupillary defect, not a hemianopia respecting the vertical midline.

question: Patient known MS, Unilateral INO, few days later, developed bilateral adduction limitation and XT. Where is the lesion:
explanation: Wall-Eyed Bilateral Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia exists when there is bilateral damage to the MLF.[11] This damage causes a primary position exotropia (eyes are looking at the opposite "wall.", thus the possibly outdated term "wall-eyed"). - Eyewiki

review.explanation: Bilateral adduction deficits with a large-angle primary position exotropia constitute the wall-eyed bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia syndrome, and it requires damage to both medial longitudinal fasciculi, which is entirely expected in demyelinating disease that has already produced a unilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia. The exotropia arises because the medial rectus subnuclei lose their tonic convergence input while abduction remains intact. A combined medial longitudinal fasciculus and contralateral paramedian pontine reticular formation lesion produces the one-and-a-half syndrome, in which one eye cannot move horizontally at all and the other retains only abduction with nystagmus, a very different picture from symmetric bilateral adduction failure. Neither option involving a paramedian pontine reticular formation lesion fits a patient who can still abduct both eyes.

referenceLinks.title: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
referenceLinks.shows: Ocular findings in ~90% (periorbital oedema, chemosis, proptosis, progressive ophthalmoplegia) and management with broad-spectrum antimicrobials as primary therapy, anticoagulation only as adjunct

referenceLinks.title: Cavernous Sinus Syndrome — EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Imaging and clinical signs of cavernous sinus pathology including thrombosis, proptosis and chemosis

referenceLinks.title: Horner Syndrome — EyeWiki

figureFinding: Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis — proptosis, chemosis, periorbital oedema and multiple cranial neuropathies (ophthalmoplegia); antibiotics are the first-line treatment

review.explanation: Reading option C as the real stem, a patient with cavernous sinus thrombosis who is not alert has presumed septic thrombosis and needs immediate broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci and anaerobes, with attention to the source, usually sinusitis or a facial or dental infection. Antibiotics are the intervention that changes mortality and must not wait for imaging or cultures beyond taking blood cultures. Anticoagulation is used by many centres and may reduce propagation of the thrombus, but the evidence is weaker, the intracranial haemorrhage risk is real, and it is never the first thing given. In a patient with declining consciousness the immediate priorities are antibiotics, airway and neurological support, and neurosurgical or ENT drainage of the source.
review.concern: The question field contains text about cocaine pupil testing for Horner syndrome, which belongs to a different item, and the actual stem is embedded in option C. Answer given on the recoverable clinical question.

question: Which will tell you that it is non-organic visual loss?
explanation: See self assessment below:

review.explanation: An optokinetic response to a rotating drum is objective proof that the visual pathway is intact enough to generate pursuit and refixation, which establishes vision of at least around 20/400 and cannot be voluntarily suppressed by most patients. That positive demonstration of function is what unmasks non-organic visual loss. A mirror test showing no movement points the other way, since a seeing patient reflexively follows their own image; absent movement is what a truly blind eye would show. Absence of a relative afferent pupillary defect in a patient claiming dense unilateral loss is a genuine and useful clue, but it is weaker evidence because bilateral symmetric disease, media opacity, amblyopia and cortical lesions can all cause visual loss without an afferent defect, so it excludes rather than proves.

question: No pictures. There was a similar question in Ophthquestions. In children, you want to use the executive type: Pseudophakia, you did refraction with retinoscopy without a lens, showed wide beam and fast "with" movement in all direction. What is his refraction:
explanation: Most likely the answer is B if the WD is 50cm. JCC last step Hyperope underwent cataract surgery in one eye has difficulty seeing. Refraction was hyperopic in one eye and myopic in the other eye with 20/20 vision OU: Give contact lenses; Slab off prism.

review.explanation: With movement means the far point of the eye lies behind the examiner, so the eye is either hyperopic, emmetropic, or myopic by less than the dioptric equivalent of the working distance. A wide, bright and fast reflex indicates you are close to neutrality, and if neutrality is essentially reached with no lens in place at a fifty centimetre working distance, the gross finding of plano must have the two dioptres of working distance subtracted, giving a net refraction of minus two. This is the standard trap: forgetting to subtract the working distance leaves you reporting plano. The answer depends entirely on the working distance being fifty centimetres; at sixty-seven centimetres the answer would be minus one point five.
review.concern: The entry is a merged recall containing fragments of at least three separate questions (executive bifocals in children, this retinoscopy item, and a Jackson cross cylinder or slab-off item). The working distance is not stated in the recalled stem, and the answer is only determinate if it is fifty centimetres.

question: Aphakic patient with +15 diopter in one eye wearing CL but complain of anisokonia what to do?

options.A: Reduce the CL to +12 and make him wear +3 glasses.
options.B: Increase the CL to +18 and make him wear -3 glasses
options.C: Investigate for other causes of anisokonia as CL doesn't cause it.

explanation: or choice D C or better measurements by exclusion since choice A and B are incorrect. Reducing the power of the contact lens to +12 diopters and making the patient wear +3 glasses may not be the best option as this can cause significant aniseikonia and distortion of the images. increasing the power of the contact lens in the affected eye to +18 diopters and making the patient wear -3 glasses to balance the magnification between the two eyes. may not be feasible or comfortable for the patient as it can cause significant discomfort and adaptation issues. Anisokonia caused by vertex distance with CL there is no VD bifocals in children:

review.explanation: Correcting unilateral aphakia with a contact lens reduces aniseikonia from the roughly twenty-five percent produced by spectacles to about seven percent, which is still above the five percent threshold at which most patients become symptomatic, so residual aniseikonia with a contact lens is expected rather than unexplained. To reduce it further you overplus the contact lens and neutralise the excess with a minus spectacle lens, creating a reverse Galilean telescope in which light passes first through the minus lens and then the plus lens, producing net minification of the retinal image. That is exactly what a plus eighteen contact lens with a minus three spectacle does, and it is a recognised iseikonic technique. Option A does the reverse, shifting plus power out to the spectacle plane, which increases magnification and would make the symptoms worse.
review.concern: The source answer states that a contact lens does not cause aniseikonia, which is not correct as an absolute. Aphakia is a refractive rather than axial ametropia, so by Knapp's law the contact lens minimises but does not abolish the image size disparity, and the residual is typically around seven percent, well within the symptomatic range. The optical principle supporting B is the reverse Galilean telescope: a plus lens at the corneal plane combined with a minus lens at the spectacle plane, separated by the vertex distance, minifies the image. I acknowledge the source's practical objection that the combination can be poorly tolerated, which is why an intraocular lens or secondary implant is usually the definitive answer in real practice, but among the three options offered B is the optically correct manoeuvre and C is a false statement.

question: Pathology slide: Child with lower lid lesion, biopsy showed keratin filled cavity lined by keratinized squamous epithelium:
explanation: Epidermoid cysts, also known as a sebaceous cysts, are encapsulated subepidermal nodules filled with keratin. Here is a pathology slide of it:

review.explanation: A cavity lined by keratinised stratified squamous epithelium and filled with lamellated keratin is the textbook histology of an epidermal inclusion or epidermoid cyst, which is by far the commonest lid cyst in a child. Keratoacanthoma also contains a central keratin plug but shows a cup-shaped crater with buttressing epidermal lips and proliferating, glassy squamous epithelium with a chronic inflammatory infiltrate at the base, and it arises in sun-damaged adult skin. Squamous cell carcinoma shows atypical squamous cells invading the dermis in irregular nests with keratin pearls and dyskeratosis, not a bland epithelial lining. The key discriminator on the slide is that the epithelial lining in an epidermoid cyst is orderly and mature, with an intact granular layer and no cytological atypia.

question: MFKPs composition:
explanation: Mutton fat KPs are composed of Macrophages, while small KPs are composed of lymphocytes. Choroidal hemangioma histopathology and fundus photo. No choices or pictures. Here are examples: Pathology slide: PAM; Nevus; Melanoma; Normal conj.

review.explanation: Mutton-fat keratic precipitates are the hallmark of granulomatous inflammation and are composed of macrophages together with the epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells they transform into, which is why they appear large, greasy and yellowish on the endothelium. Fine, small keratic precipitates by contrast are made of lymphocytes and neutrophils and signify non-granulomatous inflammation. Their presence should redirect the differential towards sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, syphilis, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease and sympathetic ophthalmia. Note that epithelioid cells are simply activated macrophages, so option D is not strictly wrong; macrophages is the more inclusive and conventionally expected answer.

question: Pathology slide: BCC what would the pt have before biopsy:
explanation: Most likely B Nodular BCC (the most common type) presents with a white or pink, dome-shaped papule with pearly border. The 4 most common causes of chronic conjunctivitis are: Inclusion conjunctivitis (chlamydia), Trachoma (Chlamydia), molluscum contagiosum (will go by itself in 6-12 months), and medications (e.g., glaucoma medications). Signs and symptoms of BCC include: Ulceration and bleeding; Non-healing skin lesion; Skin crusting; Paresthesia or anesthesia; Eyelash loss (madarosis); Distortion of normal eyelid margin or tissue architecture

review.explanation: Nodular basal cell carcinoma, the commonest periocular skin malignancy and the commonest type of basal cell carcinoma, presents clinically as a pearly, raised papule with rolled telangiectatic borders and often central ulceration, so that is what the patient would have shown before biopsy. Histologically it corresponds to nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artefact from the surrounding stroma. Chronic keratoconjunctivitis is a red herring; its common causes are chlamydial infection, trachoma, molluscum and topical medication toxicity, and it is not a precursor to basal cell carcinoma. Other clinical red flags for a lid malignancy are madarosis, distortion of the lid margin architecture and a non-healing ulcer.

question: Pathology slide: Lower lid ulcerated mass, you took biopsy, what's the diagnosis?
explanation: Most likely A This is most likely a case of squamous cell carcinoma, because of the keratin pearls that are seen in the pathology slide. - PAM (other options nevus, melanoma, normal conj) A PAM (Fig. 2B) without atypia is best characterized by minimal melanocytic hyperplasia along the basal epithelial layer of the conjunctival. PAM with atypia shows usually isolated or confluent nests of atypical melanocytes. Pagetoid spread can also be observed. The melanocytes exhibit varying signs of atypia as large abnormal cells, prominent nucleoli, a high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, and mitotic figures. AAO Try this site to navigate pathology slide: https://secure.aao.org/zoomify/ConjunctivaPAM_with_mild_atypia_c_min_with_atypia_Milma n.htm Friedman - epidermoid cyst Reference: Yanoff ocular pathology BCC slide what would the pt have before biopsy

review.explanation: If the slide shows keratin pearls, that is squamous cell carcinoma: invasive nests of atypical squamous cells with intercellular bridges and concentric whorls of keratinisation extending into the dermis. Basal cell carcinoma would instead show basaloid nests with peripheral palisading and a cleft between tumour and stroma, and no keratin pearls. Seborrhoeic keratosis is a benign acanthotic proliferation with horn cysts and no invasion or atypia, and sebaceous carcinoma shows foamy, lipid-laden cytoplasm with pagetoid spread into the overlying epithelium and is best identified with a lipid stain on fresh tissue. Clinically an ulcerated lower lid mass is more often basal cell carcinoma, so this item is decided by the histology, not the location.
review.concern: The answer depends entirely on a pathology slide that is not available to me. The stem describes only an ulcerated lower lid mass, which on frequency alone would favour basal cell carcinoma; I am agreeing with A on the strength of the source's description of keratin pearls, which cannot be independently verified here.

question: Child with fair skin and kinky hair, parents normal, paternal uncle has the same. Chance of sibling having the same?
explanation: Autosomal recessive Autosomal recessive Red urine

review.explanation: Unaffected parents with an affected child indicate that both parents are carriers, which is autosomal recessive transmission, giving each subsequent sibling a one in four recurrence risk. The affected relative on the paternal side argues against X-linked recessive inheritance, in which affected males cluster on the maternal side through carrier mothers. Fair skin with fine, brittle, light hair in a child fits homocystinuria, which also carries ectopia lentis, a marfanoid habitus, developmental delay and a serious thromboembolic risk, and is autosomal recessive. Fifty percent would apply to autosomal dominant disease with an affected parent, and less than one percent would suggest a sporadic or new mutation event, neither of which fits this pedigree.
